headline: AURA ENERGY'S TIRIS BFS DELIVERS $500M NPV AT $90 URANIUM — DECEMBER FINAL INVESTMENT DECISION TARGETED
snippet: Aura Energy (ASX: AEE) completed the Bankable Feasibility Study for its Tiris uranium project in Mauritania on October 16, reporting a post-tax NPV of US$500.3M at US$90/lb U3O8 and a 28% post-tax IRR with 3.2-year payback. Development capital is US$349.8M and the 26-year mine life targets average annual production of 1.8 million lbs U3O8. Aura is now targeting a Final Investment Decision in December 2026, contingent on finalising a senior debt facility with the US International Development Finance Corporation ($150–170M under negotiation) and completing remaining project finance arrangements. At $90/lb — which is now below the spot price of $89.63/lb and well below the long-term contract price of $96.50/lb — the BFS economics are robust, and the December FID timetable would put first production by end-2028 if approved. For investors in uranium development stories, Tiris represents one of the few projects globally with a completed BFS, a named utility offtake MoU, and a clear path to financing and construction inside this decade.

headline: URANIUM LONG-TERM CONTRACT PRICE HITS $96.50/LB — SURPASSES 2007 PEAK FOR FIRST TIME IN 19 YEARS
snippet: The uranium long-term contract price as reported for September 2026 reached US$96.50/lb — surpassing the $95/lb peak from the 2007 uranium bull cycle and reaching an 18-to-19-year high. Spot uranium ended September at $89.63/lb. The term-over-spot premium of roughly $9/lb reflects utilities paying up for long-dated supply certainty, an increasingly important signal for the junior uranium sector: when utilities enter long-term contracts above spot, it validates the structural demand thesis and validates the economics of projects that require 7–10 years of development before first uranium delivery. A key context: Cameco shares are down about 6.9% for the year despite the contract price milestone — a disconnect between physical demand fundamentals and equity market sentiment that may represent an opportunity for investors focused on development-stage projects where valuations lag contract-price improvements.

headline: JAGUAR URANIUM: MAIDEN 14.3M LB RESOURCE AT LAGUNA SALADA — COVERS JUST 4.3% OF 210,000-HA ARGENTINA PROJECT
snippet: Jaguar Uranium (TSX-V) announced on October 13 a maiden mineral resource estimate at its Laguna Salada project in Patagonia, Argentina, totalling 4.2 million lbs of Indicated U3O8 and 10.1 million lbs of Inferred U3O8, plus a significant vanadium co-product of 31.1 million lbs Indicated and 57.3 million lbs Inferred V2O5. The resource covers approximately 4.3% of Jaguar's 210,284-hectare land package, suggesting material expansion potential with further drilling. The company holds nearly US$18 million in cash and no debt. Argentina's regulatory reforms under the Milei government have streamlined mining approvals, and the Patagonian uranium/vanadium corridor has become an increasingly active exploration theatre. The vanadium component — used in grid-scale battery storage — adds optionality value beyond uranium alone, and the small footprint of the maiden estimate relative to the total property makes this a meaningful first milestone rather than the ceiling of the resource.

headline: EXIRO NICKEL CLOSES VALE THOMPSON ACQUISITION — NICKEL BELT IN NORTHERN MANITOBA UNDER NEW OWNERSHIP
snippet: Exiro Nickel announced on October 16 the completion of its acquisition of Vale Base Metals' Thompson mine and concentrator in northern Manitoba — the first major ownership change at Thompson in decades. Vale retains an 18.9% equity stake in the new Exiro Nickel Company alongside a multi-year nickel concentrate offtake agreement and up to US$200 million in contingent payments tied to future nickel prices. The deal, originally announced in February 2026, was backed by a Orion-led consortium with US$200 million in initial financing. The Thompson Nickel Belt is one of the highest-grade nickel regions in North America, and the transaction signals that institutional capital is willing to invest in Canadian nickel assets despite weak spot prices near $15,000/tonne. For junior nickel explorers in the Thompson belt, the deal's completion crystallises a new exploration and development paradigm at the region's flagship asset and may stimulate renewed interest in surrounding exploration land.

headline: BHP AVERTS ESCONDIDA STRIKE WITH NEW 3-YEAR SUPERVISORS' DEAL — WORLD'S LARGEST COPPER MINE STAYS OPEN
snippet: BHP and the supervisors' union at Escondida — the world's largest copper mine in Chile — reached a new 36-month collective agreement on October 14-15, with 64% of union members accepting improved pay and benefits and a strike threat averted. The deal resolves near-term supply disruption risk at a mine that produces over 1.1 million tonnes of copper per year — roughly 5% of global mine supply. The outcome is slightly positive for copper prices, removing a near-term supply shock that had contributed to LME copper reaching US$14,436/t mid-week before the CPI-driven sell-off. For junior copper explorers, the bigger picture is unchanged: Chilean mines keep narrowly avoiding disruptions but remain structurally constrained by ageing infrastructure, deeper ore, lower grades, and ongoing labour tensions — reinforcing the strategic case for new mine supply in less labour-contested jurisdictions such as Canada, Peru, and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

headline: LUCA MINING CLOSES C$211M FINANCING FOR CAPSTONE'S COZAMIN COPPER-SILVER MINE — DEAL ON TRACK FOR Q4
snippet: Luca Mining announced October 14 the completion of C$211 million in subscription receipt financings — including a $40 million private placement from Wheaton Precious Metals and Taurus Mining Finance Fund No. 3 alongside a bought-deal placement — clearing a key milestone in its US$290-million-upfront acquisition of Capstone Copper's Cozamin mine in Zacatecas, Mexico. The total deal value is up to US$385 million including contingent copper-price-linked payments through 2029. Cozamin is a 20-year producing underground copper-silver mine that Luca says will more than double its 2027 production profile. The closing of the financing confirms deal certainty ahead of the Q4 2026 transaction close. For investors tracking mid-tier copper consolidation, the Cozamin deal represents a model for acquiring cash-generating producing assets rather than development-stage projects — a strategy that de-risks balance sheet exposure during a volatile copper price environment while still providing meaningful production growth.

headline: TRUMP: 'MASSIVE' OIL, GAS AND MINERAL EXPLORATION IN GREENLAND SET TO BEGIN — BUT ANALYSTS SAY 'IT'S NOT THAT SIMPLE'
snippet: President Trump announced via Truth Social on October 14 that 'massive' exploration for oil, gas and minerals in Greenland is 'set to begin' — a statement that moved rare earth stocks but offered no specific projects, permits, operators, or timelines. Critical Metals (NASDAQ: CRML) rose 4% in morning trading on its Tanbreez rare earths project in southern Greenland, which already holds formal government mining approvals through 2050 and a US$120 million letter of interest from the US Export-Import Bank. However, BNN Bloomberg and AP both caution that the September 22 US-Greenland-Denmark defence agreement grants the US no special exploration rights, Greenland's Parliament has not rescinded its 2021 uranium exploration ban, and the island's remote infrastructure and harsh climate have defeated previous development attempts. The announcement is best read as a geopolitical signal — the US wants Greenland's rare earth and critical mineral assets as a counter to China's export control dominance — rather than an imminent operational programme.

headline: GREENLAND MINERS WELCOME TRUMP'S PLAN — TANBREEZ, AUKING REACT AS CRML SEEKS PILOT PLANT THIS YEAR
snippet: Mining Weekly reported October 15 that Greenland-focused developers AuKing Mining and Critical Metals (CRML) both welcomed Trump's October 14 Greenland mineral exploration statement, with Critical Metals moving most directly to capitalise: the company's Tanbreez mine holds formal Greenlandic government mining approvals through 2050, a US$120 million Export-Import Bank letter of interest, and plans to launch a pilot facility before year-end 2026. The US-Greenland defence partnership signed September 22 limits investment by non-NATO countries in strategic Greenlandic sectors — a measure that effectively walls off Chinese capital and benefits the US-aligned developers currently holding exploration and mining concessions. For investors in rare earth stocks, the Tanbreez approval and EXIM Bank interest represent the most tangible near-term catalyst: a pilot plant launch would be the first step toward establishing a non-Chinese source of heavy rare earths in a NATO-aligned jurisdiction.

headline: US PROJECT VAULT READIES 'SEVERAL HUNDRED MILLION TO $1 BILLION' IN LOANS FOR CRITICAL MINERALS MANUFACTURERS
snippet: VaultCo — the private manager of the US government's Project Vault critical minerals reserve — is in talks with more than 70 companies and expects to announce a first tranche of loans to original equipment manufacturers in the 'several hundred million to potentially $1 billion' range, according to executive chairman Brett Lambert. The reserve, announced in February 2026 as a $12 billion public-private partnership, has already accepted an initial delivery of 12,000 metric tonnes of Congolese copper from Mercuria. Target minerals include antimony, cobalt, copper, graphite, lead, nickel and silicon. The manufacturer lending programme represents the demand-side of the equation: by providing subsidised loans for domestic fabrication capacity, Project Vault attempts to create a full-supply-chain incentive that makes North American critical mineral production economically viable even against Chinese competition. For junior miners in cobalt, graphite, nickel and copper, an operational federal offtake and financing ecosystem is a meaningful de-risking of the commercial pathway for any project that can credibly supply the reserve's target commodities.

headline: TOP 50 MINING COMPANIES LOSE $264B AS GOLD TRADE UNWINDS AND LITHIUM STOCKS EXIT THE INDEX — MINING.COM Q3
snippet: Mining.com's quarterly review of the world's 50 largest mining companies by market capitalisation reports the group lost US$264 billion in combined value during Q3 2026, as gold equities corrected sharply from their 2026 highs and lithium companies fell out of the top 50 entirely — leaving only three lithium names versus six at the 2022 peak. The gold equity correction reflects the disconnect between record gold prices near $4,100–$5,500 earlier in the year and the equity market's repricing of producer costs, rate hike risk, and geopolitical uncertainty. The lithium exit illustrates the brutal cycle speed of battery metals: the five lithium companies that sat in the top 50 at the 2022 peak collectively shed roughly $65 billion over four years. For retail mining investors, the Q3 data reinforces a key lesson: sector-level fund outflows create indiscriminate selling that divorces equity prices from fundamental project values — which historically precedes the most asymmetric recovery opportunities for investors willing to hold quality assets through the drawdown.

headline: SWEDEN URANIUM BAN REPEALED — BUT HÄGGÅN AND VIKEN PROJECTS ARE STILL 15 YEARS FROM ANY PRODUCTION
snippet: A Discovery Alert analysis in mid-October 2026 examines the reality behind Sweden's uranium mining ban repeal — effective January 1, 2026 — and concludes that the country's two largest uranium projects, Häggån and Viken, remain at least 15 years from any meaningful production. The piece traces why: Sweden's Minerals Act permitting process for a new uranium mine runs a decade or more even with political support; a separate proposal to remove the classification of uranium mining as a 'nuclear installation' was still under consultation; and infrastructure for uranium extraction and processing does not exist in the country. For junior uranium investors tracking jurisdiction diversification thesis, the analysis is a useful calibration: Sweden's ban repeal has symbolic importance for European nuclear sovereignty and opens exploration, but it does not add near-term supply to the market. Developers including District Metals (TSX-V: DMX) can now advance field work, but investors should model first Swedish uranium production no earlier than the late 2030s — which means existing production jurisdictions (Kazakhstan, Canada, Namibia, Australia) retain their scarcity premium through the current demand cycle.
